name: Henry V of England
summary: Henry V was king of England from 1413 to 1422 and the English commander at Agincourt. His campaigns revived English fortunes in the Hundred Years’ War.
details: King of England whose campaigns in France culminated in Agincourt and the Treaty of Troyes.
title: king of England

death.circumstance: Died of illness at the Chateau de Vincennes in 1422 while campaigning in France; his infant son inherited a fragile dual-monarchy project.

overview: Henry V was king of England from 1413 to 1422 and the most successful English commander of the Lancastrian phase of the Hundred Years' War. His reign joined domestic consolidation with an ambitious invasion of France that culminated in the victory at Agincourt.

His military success led to the Treaty of Troyes, which recognized him as heir to the French throne, but his death in 1422 left the project to an infant son and overextended governors. Henry's reputation was later magnified by royal propaganda, chronicles, and Shakespeare, while the historical king remains a hard-edged ruler of war finance, siegecraft, and dynastic claim-making.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Henry V was king of England from 1413 to 1422 and the most successful English commander of the Lancastrian phase of the Hundred Years' War. His reign joined domestic consolidation with an ambitious invasion of France that culminated in the victory at Agincourt.

His military success led to the Treaty of Troyes, which recognized him as heir to the French throne, but his death in 1422 left the project to an infant son and overextended governors. Henry's reputation was later magnified by royal propaganda, chronicles, and Shakespeare, while the historical king remains a hard-edged ruler of war finance, siegecraft, and dynastic claim-making.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Henry was born in 1386, probably at Monmouth Castle, into the Lancastrian branch of the Plantagenet dynasty. His father, Henry Bolingbroke, seized the English throne as Henry IV in 1399, making the younger Henry heir to a dynasty that needed military success and political legitimacy.

As prince of Wales, Henry gained practical military experience during the Glyndwr rebellion and in campaigns against powerful northern opponents. Those years taught him siegecraft, frontier politics, and the importance of noble loyalty before he inherited the crown.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Henry V of England is remembered as the model of the disciplined warrior-king, and contemporary and near-contemporary sources present a ruler of formidable seriousness, piety, and command. After a reportedly wild youth, he is said to have transformed on his accession into a grave, devout, and rigorously self-controlled monarch — a reformation of character that chroniclers emphasised and that Shakespeare later made famous.

His personality expressed itself in relentless discipline and religious conviction: he enforced strict order in his armies, attributed his stunning victory at the Battle of Agincourt to God, and pursued the conquest of France with cold, methodical determination, including the harsh treatment of besieged towns. Admirers saw justice and resolve; the same qualities could appear as severity, as in the killing of prisoners at Agincourt and the unbending prosecution of his claims.

The portrait is shaped partly by patriotic memory of England's greatest medieval military triumph, but it is well grounded: a pious, austere, intensely focused ruler whose self-mastery and martial competence made him formidable. He is remembered as the embodiment of righteous, disciplined kingship — admirable and hard in equal measure.

contentSections.title: As king of England
paragraphs: Henry became king in 1413 and moved quickly to present himself as a disciplined, orthodox, and martial ruler. He suppressed the Oldcastle rising, managed aristocratic tensions, and revived English claims in France as a way to assert royal authority at home and abroad.

In 1415 he captured Harfleur after a costly siege, then marched across northern France toward Calais. At Agincourt his exhausted army took a defensive position on narrow, muddy ground, where English archers and dismounted men-at-arms shattered repeated French assaults.

Henry returned to France in 1417 and pursued a more systematic conquest of Normandy. The Treaty of Troyes in 1420 married him to Catherine of Valois and recognized him as heir to Charles VI, but the settlement depended on continued military pressure and Burgundian cooperation.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Henry died of illness at the Chateau de Vincennes on 31 August 1422 while campaigning in France. His death came only weeks before Charles VI of France died, leaving Henry's infant son Henry VI as the nominal heir to both kingdoms.

The timing exposed the fragility of the dual-monarchy project. English commanders could still win battles and hold territory, but they lacked Henry's authority and faced persistent French resistance around the Valois cause.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Henry's legacy rests on the dramatic contrast between military brilliance and political impermanence. Agincourt became one of England's most famous battlefield victories, while the wider conquest of France collapsed within a generation.

Later literature turned Henry into a model warrior-king, but the archive has to keep that memory beside the harder realities of siege warfare, taxation, prisoner killing at Agincourt, and the contested legality of Lancastrian claims in France.

keyAchievements.title: Won the Battle of Agincourt
keyAchievements.description: Henry’s victory at Agincourt turned a dangerous campaign into a major Lancastrian triumph and propaganda success.

keyAchievements.title: Secured the Treaty of Troyes
keyAchievements.description: The Treaty of Troyes recognized Henry as heir to the French throne, though the settlement collapsed after his early death.

keyAchievements.title: Restored Lancastrian royal authority
keyAchievements.description: Military victory and disciplined kingship helped Henry recover prestige after the instability of his father’s reign.
